title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: one in the morning, a review doc, two verdicts and one heat: the Gita calls it fever
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: after all that teaching, what does Krishna finally hand Arjuna?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma under review: consequence, cost, harm and strength, and no scoreboard of credit. Today, the one holding the pen, and a heat.

One in the morning. The review doc is open, the screen is the only light, and the face over it is hot. Two verdicts take turns. I did so much. I did nothing right. Different words, the same heat behind both, the kind that makes a pillow feel warm on both sides. The Gita has a word for that heat, and it's a plain, bodily one. Fever.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `TWO VERDICTS, ONE HEAT.` → `THE GITA CALLS IT FEVER.`

segments.voice: In chapter three, Krishna tells Arjuna, in paraphrase: offering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free of craving and of the sense of mine, act, and let the fever go. The Sanskrit is vigatajvara, the fever gone. Jvara is the ordinary word for a fever, the kind a hand on the forehead can feel. A few verses earlier he says where the heat comes from. All actions are done by the strands of nature, he says; the one confused by ego thinks, I am the doer. That doesn't mean nobody is responsible. It means an action is bigger than one will: the body that had the strength, the people who showed up, the weather, the bus that came on time. A fevered review swings between the two verdicts, look what I did, look how I failed, and both put the reviewer in the middle of the story. The cool review asks yesterday's questions honestly. It owns the mistakes and fixes them. It doesn't take the year's good as a trophy, or its failures as a sentence. Some Hindus on the path of devotion offer the work to God. Others hold it more simply, as work handed on to the world. Either way, the doer steps a little out of the middle, and the review comes down to a livable temperature: cooler, clearer, kinder.
screen: `VIGATAJVARA: THE FEVER GONE.` · `I AM THE DOER, SAYS EGO.` · `NO TROPHY, NO SENTENCE.` · then, large: `COOLER, CLEARER, KINDER.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, hold the glass a moment and feel its coolness in your palm, then take one slow sip and follow the cool down. If there's none, rest the back of a hand against your cheek. Then breathe, and notice the air cool on the way in and warm on the way out.
Karma, without fever: the work owned, its mistakes fixed, and the doer a little out of the middle.
Your line: karma, a year designed and reviewed, and looked back on cool. One day left in the capstone.

screen: `DAY 1656 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES KRISHNA HAND BACK?`

howItsDone: Hindu teachers who draw on Gita 3.27–30 counsel doing one's work wholeheartedly while letting go of the sense of being its only author; some offer each day's work to God before or after it.

fork.setup: your team loses the final, and the captain, your friend, texts: 'it's all on me.' what does Gita chapter three suggest you tell her?
options: agree. owning it fully is the honest thing.
own a fix, but the game was bigger than one will.

fork.reveal: actions are done by many strands, the Gita says; ego thinks, I alone did it. owning a fix is honest. carrying the whole loss is fever.

original.note: Sanskrit vigatajvara: vigata, gone, and jvara, fever. In Gita 3.30, act with the fever gone.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good review means feeling either proud or guilty.
what it means: own the mistakes and fix them, but let the heat of trophy and sentence go.
what a scholar hears: Gita 3.30, yudhyasva vigatajvarah, fight with the fever gone; and 3.27, the one deluded by ahamkara thinks 'I am the doer.'
recall: measured, so the work can last

chat.meaning: Krishna asks for work done with the fever gone: neither trophy nor sentence, since an action is bigger than one will.
